drafts.topic: The Economist's subscription offer: how a "pointless" print-only option sold more bundles

post.hook: Why did a useless print-only option boost bundles?
slides: The Economist added a $199 **print-only** subscription in 2018, alongside its digital-only $149 plan and a $299 **print + digital** bundle. The print-only tier received almost no sign-ups.
Psychology calls this the **contrast effect**: an option that is clearly inferior makes another, slightly pricier option look more attractive.
When prospects compare $199 print-only to $299 print + digital, the bundle appears to offer **double the value for only $100 more**, triggering a perception of a better deal.

Marketers can mimic this by introducing a **deliberately weaker tier**, for example, a basic plan with limited features at a price close to the premium option, so the premium feels like a clear upgrade.
Small businesses can test a **“good-enough”** version of a product at a price just below their main offer; it nudges customers toward the higher-margin package without extra persuasion.
post.takeaway: Add a modestly priced, clearly lesser option to make your primary offering look like the smarter choice. Keep the decoy simple and inexpensive so it doesn’t cannibalize sales.
post.caption:
The Economist’s clever trick shows how a barely-wanted print-only tier can push readers into a richer bundle. By placing an option that looks good enough, but not great, they made the premium bundle feel like a no-brainer. 

You don’t need a massive catalog to use this trick. A single “good-enough” tier can sharpen the appeal of your main product, especially when the price gap highlights extra value. 

Try adding a modest, less-featured version of your service and watch the upgrade rate climb. 

What’s the weakest tier you could launch tomorrow to make your premium shine?

drafts.topic: "Submit" buttons: why first-person CTAs like "Start my free trial" get more clicks

post.hook: Why do first-person buttons click more?
slides: Before: **Get started** – a generic button that tells the prospect what to do, but not why it matters to them.
It falls flat because prospects see it as a directive, not a personal invitation. The brain prioritizes information linked to the self.
Enter the **Self-Reference Effect** – we remember and prefer content that mentions ourselves.
After: **Start my free trial** – the button names the user, making the action feel like a personal benefit.
Now the prospect envisions themselves enjoying the trial, so the click feels like a low-risk, self-focused decision.
post.takeaway: Rewrite CTAs in the first person. Turn commands into personal invitations like “Try my free sample” or “Claim my discount” to boost clicks.
post.caption:
Ever wonder why some buttons get more love than others? It’s not magic – it’s psychology. When you speak directly to the reader, their brain lights up, treating the offer as personal.

We’ve swapped a bland “Get started” for a first-person “Start my free trial.” The difference? The Self-Reference Effect, which makes self-related words stick in memory and feel more relevant.

Try swapping one generic CTA on your site today and watch the clicks climb. Which button will you rewrite first?

fact_check.claim: Self‑Reference Effect causes people to remember self‑related information better
fact_check.source: Rogers, T.B. et al., 1977, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
A/B tests reported by various SaaS companies, 2020‑2022
